basis: The printing heads this quaestio 'VERS. 16.' and it opens '(Vers. 16 et seqq.) Dan judicabit populum suum, sicut unum de sceptris Israel. Fiat Dan'. The chapter is Migne's caput, carried from the last one the printing states, and the lemma raises nothing against it.
date_basis: Written at Bethlehem and named in Jerome's own De viris illustribus 135, finished in 393, among the works already published; the preface announces it as the first of a series of Hebrew Questions on the whole of Scripture that he never continued. The early 390s is as close as the evidence held here reaches. The date is the writing, not the 1845 printing and not Vallarsi's 1767 edition.
text: (Vers. 16 et seqq.) Dan judicabit populum suum, sicut unum de sceptris Israel. Fiat Dan coluber in via, regulus in semita, mordens ungulas equi, ut cadat [Al. et cadet] ascensor ejus retrorsum: salvatorem tuum exspectabo, Domine. Samson judex in Israel, de tribu Dan fuit. Hoc ergo dicit: Nunc videns in spiritu comam nutrire Samson Nazaraeum tuum, caesisque hostibus triumphare; quod in similitudinem colubri regulique obsidentis vias, nullum per terram Israel transire permittat: sed [Al. sicut] etiam si quis temerarius virtute sua, quasi equi velocitate confisus, eam voluerit praedonis more populari, effugere non valebit. Totum autem per metaphoram serpentis et equitis loquitur. Videns ergo tam fortem Nazaraeum tuum, quod et ipse propter meretricem mortuus est, et moriens nostros occidit inimicos, putavi, O Deus, ipsum esse Christum Filium tuum; verum quia mortuus est, et non resurrexit, et rursum captivus ductus est Israel, alius mihi Salvator mundi, et mei generis praestolandus est, Ut veniat cui repositum est et ipse erit exspectatio gentium.
